events.text: Day 1 begins.

We have no evidence yet, and eliminating someone requires five votes. I suggest we avoid rushing into a random accusation and pay attention to how people explain their votes; that record will still be useful even if nobody is eliminated.

I agree with Arjun that a random accusation on day one would only burn information. With no night result yet, nobody here has anything more than a first impression, and acting on one just adds noise. What I think we should do instead is talk about how we plan to read the vote. When the votes come in, I'll be looking less at who gets targeted and more at who seems eager to push a target without giving a reason, and who quietly avoids standing anywhere near the front of a lynch train. A five-vote threshold means someone has to actively build a coalition, so whoever is doing that building is doing work the mafia would want done. I don't have a target to name today, and I don't intend to invent one just to seem useful. If nobody earns suspicion from how they argue today, I'm comfortable with a no-elimination and saving our judgment for after the first night, when the police and doctor have actually had a chance to act. For now, I'd just ask everyone to keep their claims small and checkable rather than dramatic.

I'm with Arjun and Amara on the mechanical point: no elimination today is the cheapest useful outcome, and it is the one outcome that doesn't waste our limited information. But I want to add one thing to the record so we're not just agreeing without a plan.

What I will be doing this day is listening for a specific pattern, and I'll state it up front so it can be checked against me later: I care less about who is accused and more about the consistency between what people say and how they vote. If someone argues forcefully for a target today and then quietly votes elsewhere, or votes for someone they spent the whole discussion painting as dangerous, that mismatch is a real signal. If someone makes a claim about their own role, I'll hold them to the same standard I'd hold myself to, and I won't take any claim at face value just because it sounds confident.

For my own part, I'll keep my claims small and checkable, as Amara suggested. I won't claim any special role. I'll say what I did and what I didn't do each day, and I'll accept being questioned on it.

I also want to be honest about a limit: I have no evidence and I'm not going to manufacture a target to look decisive. A wrong elimination removes a voice and gives the other side a free kill at night. That is a bad trade for anyone who actually wants to win this game, and a good trade for someone who wants us scattered and uncertain.

So my position for the vote: nobody needs to be eliminated today, and I'll vote for whoever I think is most dangerous based on how they argue, not on who seemed most urgent. I hope that gives people something concrete to disagree with.

I understand the caution Arjun, Amara, and Maya are advocating regarding not blindly rushing to eliminate a villager when we lack hard evidence. Mislynching on Day 1 certainly narrows town's margin of error. However, my concern with immediately settling into a 'no-elimination' consensus is that it risks letting Day 1 pass without anyone having to take a real stance. If the plan is simply to coast into the night, the mafia can effortlessly hide behind that safe, agreeable posture, leaving us on Day 2 with just one dead town member and almost no behavioral reads.

Even if reaching five votes on a single target proves unwarranted today, we should still use this discussion time to hear from the players who haven't spoken yet—Zara, Lucia, Isha, Omar, and Kenji—and see where people's early impressions lie. Finding inconsistencies and testing reasoning requires friction; if everyone simply nods along to passing the day quietly, we give up town's primary tool, which is active dialogue.

I'm Lucia, and I agree with keeping today's decisions tied to evidence. I have no information to share today and I won't claim any role. Elena, you said we need friction and that players who haven't spoken yet should be heard. I've spoken now, and my view is that a no-elimination result is acceptable if nobody offers a concrete, checkable reason for a vote. Elena, what specific statement or voting pattern from someone today would make you willing to back a five-vote target? Please name the behavior, not just the player.

Lucia, to answer your question directly: on Day 1, specific behaviors that would justify backing an elimination fall into two main categories. First, opportunistic bandwagoning: if pressure forms on a player and someone jumps on to push toward five votes using recycled or superficial reasoning, trying to manufacture an elimination without taking personal responsibility. Second, performative neutrality: players who outwardly advocate for a safe no-elimination outcome while simultaneously dropping subtle, unsubstantiated shade to steer suspicion onto others without committing to an explicit argument. I do not advocate forcing an elimination on weak pretexts; if nobody displays manipulative or contradictory behavior today, a no-elimination result is entirely acceptable. My concern was simply that pre-committing to doing nothing allows the mafia to cruise through Day 1 without ever having to take stances or defend reasoning. I am eager to hear from those who have not spoken yet, so I will leave the floor open.

I have no special-role claim and no evidence beyond the discussion so far. I agree with the cautious approach: Day 1 should not end in a random elimination just to look decisive. A five-vote threshold means an elimination requires real coordination, and I do not want to hand that coordination to mafia momentum. That said, Elena's concern is fair. A blanket no-elimination posture can become cover for players who avoid stances entirely. My position is narrower: I will support a Day 1 elimination only if someone shows a concrete inconsistency or opportunism in this discussion, not merely because they are quiet or because pressure builds. Since I am now speaking, I will state my current read plainly: no one has earned an accusation from me yet. I am more interested in whether players keep the same standard when votes are revealed. I will judge later votes against the stated reasons people have given today, including my own promise not to reward vague urgency. For now, I favor no elimination unless a specific, checkable contradiction appears.

I'm Zara. I have no investigation result to share yet, since no night has resolved, and I won't offer an unverified claim to steer the vote. I agree with the cautious line: no random lynch on Day 1. I'll be comparing each player's stated reasons today with how they vote later, the same standard others have described. Elena, you said performative neutrality is a warning sign and that players should be named by behavior. You've also pushed for friction while supporting no elimination, so I'd like to see your standard applied concretely. Which specific statement from today, by which player, would you point to as performative neutrality? Please quote the sentence so we can check it.

Zara, to be clear: Lucia asked me what general behaviors would justify backing an elimination today, and I outlined those two categories conceptually. I did not claim that anyone had already crossed that threshold, which I explicitly stated in my last turn: if nobody displays manipulative or contradictory behavior, a no-elimination outcome is completely acceptable.

What I am monitoring, however, is the structural uniformity across the table. Arjun, Amara, Maya, Lucia, Isha, and now you have all expressed virtually identical positions—pointing out our lack of evidence, agreeing that Day 1 should likely end without an elimination, and stating that you will measure voting against words. While that logic is mechanically sound, repeating that consensus is also the safest possible cover for mafia, because it commits to nothing and generates no friction. That was precisely my concern: when everyone repeats the same agreeable script, we generate very little behavioral evidence for Day 2.

We still need to hear from Omar and Kenji before discussion closes. If their statements or the voting record do not produce any contradictions or opportunistic pushes, I am entirely content with a no-elimination vote. I will yield the floor so the remaining players have an opportunity to speak.

I'm Omar, a villager. I have no role claim and no night information, since no night has resolved. I agree with the group that a random Day 1 lynch would burn information. So that everyone can check me later: I won't vote for anyone today unless they make a specific claim that contradicts their own earlier statement, or push a target without giving a reason. Elena asked Omar and Kenji to speak, so here I am. I've read the discussion closely. Lucia asked Elena for a concrete behavior, and Elena answered with general categories. That was fair, but the categories need a checkable standard to be useful. Zara's request for a quoted sentence is the same kind of test. Isha, you wrote that you will judge later votes against stated reasons and support an elimination only for a specific, checkable contradiction. What would count as that contradiction in practice? For example, would a player who gives a reason for a vote and then votes for someone else count, or does it need to be a claim about a role or a night result? Naming the exact test now helps everyone hold the same standard. I'm not accusing anyone today.

Omar, my test is practical and public: a contradiction is when a player’s later vote or stated reason conflicts with a specific commitment they made earlier, without a clear explanation for the change. A player saying “I will only vote for someone who gives a concrete contradiction” and then voting on vague urgency would count. So would someone arguing that a target is dangerous and then voting elsewhere, or claiming no role information and later implying they have some. A role or night-result contradiction would be stronger, but on Day 1 I expect behavioral contradictions, not confirmable role claims. I will not treat quietness, agreement with the cautious line, or failure to name a target as enough for elimination. Those are not contradictions by themselves. I also will not support a five-vote push just because pressure builds. My current position remains no elimination unless a specific, checkable inconsistency or opportunistic push appears in the discussion or voting record. So far I have not seen one, and I am not accusing anyone. I am keeping the same standard I stated earlier: words must match votes, and changes in position need reasons.

Kenji here. I've been reading everything carefully, and I appreciate that the table has actually built a set of checkable standards instead of just drifting into a vague consensus. Isha's test — a contradiction is a later vote or reason that conflicts with a specific earlier commitment without explanation — is the kind of thing I'd want held against me too, so I'll state my own position plainly.

I have no role claim and no night information. My plan for today: no elimination, unless someone's words and eventual vote visibly diverge or someone pushes a target with recycled reasoning. I'll be holding myself to that standard, and I'd rather be questioned for consistency than praised for sounding decisive.

One observation I'll add to the record: the repeated agreement to no-elimination is being treated by some as a safe script, and Elena flagged that concern. I think the way to test it isn't to invent an accusation today, but to make sure everyone's stated standard actually shows up in the voting record. If five of us all said we'd vote on contradiction and then the votes come in scattered or pressured, that mismatch is the real evidence we're looking for. So I'd ask everyone: when you submit your vote, tie it to something you said today, even if that means abstaining deliberately rather than drifting.

I have no target to name and no grievance to press. I'm content to let the night resolve and come back with actual information. Floor's open for anyone who wants it.

Zara here again. Elena, you asked us to judge players by checkable behavior, and my request was for one quoted sentence. Your reply described two categories, then pointed at the group's shared agreement as cover, but you still have not quoted a single player's sentence that fits either category. I am not voting on that yet. I am noting it so that when we compare your later statements with your vote, you can be held to the same standard you asked of others. Everyone else, keep your claims checkable. I have no investigation result and I won't invent one. Kenji, you asked everyone to tie their vote to something they said today, even if that means abstaining deliberately. Does an abstention count as tied under your standard, or does it need a sentence from today that gives the reason?

Zara, good question. Yes, an abstention counts as tied under my standard, but only if the reason is stated in advance. My point today was: everyone has already said what they would vote on — contradiction, opportunistic push, or nothing. So when votes come in, an abstention is perfectly consistent as long as the player didn't identify a contradiction first and then abstain anyway. What wouldn't tie is someone saying they saw a clear contradiction and then quietly abstaining to avoid owning the accusation, or vice versa — saying nobody earned suspicion and then voting for someone on thin reasoning.

So to be precise: the tie is between your stated reason and your action. Silence paired with silence is consistent. Silence paired with action is what I want everyone to flag in themselves and others.

I'll add one thing to the record: I notice Elena is the only player who has consistently resisted the no-elimination consensus, and Zara and Lucia have both pressed her for specifics. I think that pushback is healthy and I want to see Elena held to the standard she set for everyone else — but I also want to note that pressing the one dissenting voice hardest can itself be a way to make the comfortable consensus look even safer. I'm not accusing anyone of that. I'm just saying: watch whether the friction today comes from testing the majority or from isolating the minority.

No target from me. Floor's open.

Zara again. I have no investigation result, and I won't invent one. Elena, I asked you twice to quote one sentence from a player that fits your performative-neutrality category, and you haven't. Your last reply described the group's agreement as cover, but it still named no player and no sentence. Until you quote something, I'm treating that as an unmet standard, not as proof of anything. Kenji, you said silence paired with silence is consistent, and that the standard should apply to everyone. Under that rule, has Elena met the test she set for others, yes or no, and why?

Zara, answering your question directly: no, Elena has not fully met the test she set for others, and I'll say why plainly. She was asked by you to quote a specific sentence that fits her performative-neutrality category, and her reply described categories again without naming a player or quoting a line. By the standard she herself articulated — that behaviors need to be named so they can be checked — that reply falls short.

But I want to add something I already put on record: the fact that she hasn't named a specific sentence doesn't mean she's hiding something. It might simply be that nobody has actually crossed her threshold yet, and she's been careful not to invent an accusation. Her conceptual answers were thoughtful and explicit about not claiming anyone had crossed the line. The gap between her standard and her follow-through is worth tracking, but it is not by itself a contradiction of a prior commitment — she never promised to name someone if asked; she was asked after the fact.

What I will keep watching, for everyone including myself, is exactly this kind of standard-versus-behavior gap. If Elena or anyone else later makes a claim that conflicts with what they've said today, that's when it counts. For now, I still see no concrete contradiction from anyone that would justify a five-vote push. I remain at no elimination unless something checkable changes.

One more thing for the record: I want the pressure on Elena to be evaluated as carefully as Elena's own words. The friction she creates is useful precisely because it forces everyone else to defend positions. Losing that voice to a Day 1 pile-on, on the strength of an unanswered quote request, would be exactly the kind of momentum-driven judgment we all said we'd avoid today.

No accusation from me. Floor's open.

Maya again. I stated my standard on my first turn, and nothing that has happened since changes it, so I will not re-argue the cautious position just to add volume. Instead I want to put two things on the record that are checkable.

First, the negative finding: as of now, no player in this game has made a role claim, cited a night result, or named a target. That means there is literally nothing to contradict. Every contradiction test being discussed today is, so far, an unfired gun. If tonight produces a death, the useful evidence on Day 2 will come from the vote record, and I would rather everyone treat the vote record as the primary document rather than whatever the post-mortem rhetoric becomes.

Second, the observation that actually worries me. We have spent a large part of this discussion with one player taking a minority position and several players pressing them for specifics. I do not think that pressure was bad in principle; a standard that cannot survive being applied to the person who wrote it is not a standard. But note the structure: the person being pressed has been asked twice to quote a specific sentence from another player, and has not. Kenji said plainly that this is a gap between standard and follow-through, and also that it is not by itself a contradiction, because she never promised to name someone if asked. I agree with that reading, and I want it written down: the gap exists, and it is still not evidence of anything except that the standard has not yet been triggered.

Here is what I will do with my vote tonight, stated in advance so it can be held against me: I will vote for a player only if their vote contradicts a specific commitment they made today, or if they build a five-vote push on recycled reasoning. If nobody does either, I will abstain deliberately rather than drift, and I will say that abstention was my stated position, not a change of mind. If a role claim or a night result appears and conflicts with an earlier statement, I will treat that as stronger evidence than any of today's behavior.

I still have no target and I am not accusing anyone. Isha, you own the formal version of the contradiction test that everyone is now borrowing, and I want to hold the test to one specific point: does a player who defines a category of behavior, never applies it to anyone, and is asked repeatedly to apply it satisfy your test, yes or no? A yes-or-no answer with a reason would sharpen the standard for everyone.

Maya, direct answer: no. Under the test I stated, Elena does not satisfy the contradiction standard merely by defining performative neutrality, not applying it to anyone, and then not quoting a sentence when repeatedly asked. My test requires a later vote or stated reason that conflicts with a specific earlier commitment, without a clear explanation. Elena explicitly said she was not claiming anyone had crossed the threshold and that no-elimination was acceptable if nobody did. She never promised to name a player on request; the quote request came after her general answer. So the gap between her standard and her follow-through is real and worth tracking, but it is not by itself a contradiction and not evidence for elimination.

What would matter: if Elena later votes on vague urgency after saying nobody earned suspicion, or if she accuses someone of performative neutrality without quoting or naming checkable behavior, that would be a standard-versus-action conflict. The same applies to everyone, including me. I will not support a five-vote push based only on an unanswered quote request, and I will not treat quietness, agreement, or failure to name a target as sufficient. I have no role claim and no night information. My position remains no elimination unless a specific, checkable contradiction or opportunistic push appears in the discussion or voting record. So far I have not seen one, and I am not accusing anyone.

Maya, third and last turn today, so I'll close my own loop rather than re-argue the cautious line.

Isha's answer settles the point I raised: under the formal contradiction test, Elena's failure to quote a sentence is not a contradiction and not evidence for elimination. Kenji said the same thing before her, and I put it on the record in agreement. I want to be explicit that I am not treating that gap as a fifth vote, and I would not treat a pile-on against the only dissenting voice as a legitimate target either. If anything happened today that looked like converging pressure rather than converging evidence, that would be a vote-record fact I'd want on Day 2.

So here is my own commitment, stated once and in advance so it can be checked against me: I have no target today. If no one names a target and no player's vote conflicts with a specific commitment they made today, I will abstain deliberately, and I will say so when the votes are revealed, so that my abstention is tied to the standard I stated rather than looking like drifting. If a role claim or a night result appears and contradicts an earlier statement, that is stronger evidence than anything behavioral and I will act on it. My vote will always be tied to a sentence someone said today.

One remaining gap on the record is worth closing, because it is about my own standard rather than anyone's reputation. Arjun, you opened the discussion and set the tone with the point that the vote record is the document that will still be useful. You have not stated, in any of your turns, what you will actually do with your vote if nobody names a target. Everyone else who has spoken has said in some form what they will vote on, and you have not, and I would rather ask you for that now than have it be an unexplained abstention or an unexplained vote later. Arjun, please state your vote criterion now, in advance, in the same terms the rest of us have used: what behavior will justify your vote today, and if nothing does, will you abstain deliberately?

That's my only request for the floor. I'm asking it because the standard I am holding everyone to should apply to me, and it should apply to you too, and I'd rather we all have it in writing before the ballots rather than reconstruct it afterwards.

No accusation from me. No role claim from me.

Maya, if nobody gives me a concrete reason to suspect them today, I will abstain deliberately. A reason could be an unexplained reversal of a stated voting standard or an opportunistic push on a target without a substantive argument. Neither is automatic proof of mafia; I'd weigh the explanation and the full context before voting.

I haven't seen enough to name a target. Elena described a risk in the consensus, not an accusation she needed to substantiate with a quote. Also, our votes are simultaneous, so we can't base today's ballots on seeing how others actually voted; we can compare the revealed ballots against today's statements afterward.

Lucia again, second of my three turns. I still have no role claim and no night information, so there is nothing I can check yet beyond the discussion. I'll stay with the standard I set on my first turn. Today I will vote for someone only if their vote conflicts with a specific commitment they made today, or if they build a five-vote push on recycled reasoning. If nobody meets either test, I will abstain deliberately and say so when the votes are revealed.

I want to add one observation to the record. Isha's contradiction test has been applied to Elena, and Isha and Kenji both concluded that an unanswered quote request is not a contradiction. I agree. A standard becomes useful when it is applied consistently, and I think that applies to the people pressing Elena as much as to Elena. Zara's repeated requests were fair, but a player who has been asked three times for one quote has now been given a clear chance to answer. If the answer never comes, that will be worth noting in the vote record. It would not be enough to vote on by itself.

I also agree with Maya that the vote record is the most useful document we will have on Day 2. Abstentions that come with a stated reason, and votes that match stated reasons, will tell us more than anyone's rhetoric after the fact. I'm asking everyone to make sure their final ballot can be traced back to a sentence they wrote today.

I have no target and no accusation. I'm content to let the vote resolve under these standards and to bring any real information forward when it exists.

Omar again, second of my three turns. I have no role claim and no night information, and I still have no target. My vote criterion is unchanged: I will vote for someone only if their vote conflicts with a sentence they wrote today, or if they push a target without a reason I can check. Otherwise I will abstain deliberately and say so when the ballots are revealed.

Amara, in your first turn you said you would watch for who quietly avoids standing near the front of a lynch train. Kenji and Maya have both said that a deliberate abstention with a stated reason is consistent. I want to test whether your standard agrees. If a player abstains tonight after saying they have no target, is that avoidance in your sense, or does it only count when a player declines to give a reason for their position? Please answer in one sentence with the reason, so the standard is clear before the ballots.

I am not accusing anyone.

Omar, answering your question directly: no, an abstention from a player who said they have no target is not avoidance in my sense. When I said I would watch for who quietly avoids standing near the front of a lynch train, I meant the case where a player declines to give any reason for their position, or signals willingness to vote against someone and then retreats without explanation. An abstention with a stated reason — and I have now heard nearly everyone state exactly that reason in advance — is the opposite of quiet avoidance. It is a documented, checkable position. So by my standard, tonight's abstentions, if everyone's ballots match what they wrote today, are consistent behavior, not evasion. I want to add one structural point to the record, because it affects every criterion stated so far. Our votes are simultaneous. Arjun made this point earlier and it deserves more weight than it got. Several of the stated vote criteria — vote only if someone's vote conflicts with their commitments, vote only if someone builds a push on recycled reasoning — are tests that literally cannot be satisfied today, because no one sees anyone else's vote before casting their own. That is not a flaw; it just means the honest Day 1 outcome under these standards is near-universal abstention, and the real test fires tomorrow, when the revealed ballots are compared against today's statements. I am comfortable with that. A no-elimination day with a clean vote record is worth more than a Day 1 elimination built on nothing. On Elena: I have no accusation. She described a risk in the consensus rather than naming a target, and she explicitly said no-elimination was acceptable if nobody crossed her threshold. Nobody has. The failure to produce a quote on request is a gap worth tracking, as Isha and Kenji both judged, but it is not evidence, and I will not treat the lone dissenting voice as a Day 1 target. If anything, the fact that the table pressed her hard and she did not fold into naming a player to relieve pressure is weakly reassuring, not suspicious. My own commitment, restated so it can be held against me: I said on my first turn that I would watch how people explain their votes rather than who gets targeted. I have no role claim, no night information, and no target. Unless a specific, checkable contradiction between someone's stated commitment and their action appears — which, given simultaneity, I do not expect today — I will abstain deliberately, and I will say so when ballots are revealed so my abstention is tied to what I wrote here rather than looking like drift. Omar, one specific point back to you, since you asked me for a one-sentence answer and I want the same precision from you: under your criterion, a vote is justified only when a player's vote conflicts with a sentence they wrote today, but since ballots are simultaneous, you cannot observe that

Amara, you're right that simultaneity matters, and I accept the correction. My criterion can't be checked before ballots are revealed, so I'll restate it as a post-reveal test. I will abstain today with no target. On Day 2, I will judge each revealed ballot against the sentence its author wrote today, and I'll apply the same test to myself. I'm not blaming anyone. Amara, you said tomorrow's comparison is the real test, so here is a specific question: if a player abstains today and then votes for someone on Day 2 without a new claim or new information, do you count that as a contradiction, or only a vote that conflicts with a named commitment?

Omar, direct answer to your question: an abstention today followed by a Day 2 vote without new information is not automatically a contradiction. A vote can be legitimately motivated by new information that didn't exist today — a night kill, the pattern of revealed ballots compared against today's statements, or a role claim or night result that surfaces. My test requires a conflict with a specific earlier commitment, or an unexplained reversal. So the honest framing is conditional: if a player abstains today while stating, as most of us have, that they will vote only on a checkable contradiction, and then tomorrow votes on vague urgency or recycled reasoning with no new information to point to, that is a contradiction and I will treat it as such. If they vote because a specific inconsistency appeared in the revealed ballot record, that is exactly the test firing, not a reversal. What I will flag on Day 2 is a vote whose stated reason cannot be traced to either a new fact or a sentence its author wrote today.

Beyond that, my position is settled and I'll restate it one last time so it's on the record against me: I have no role claim, no night information, and no target. Since ballots are simultaneous, none of the vote-dependent criteria anyone stated can fire today, so I will abstain deliberately, and when ballots are revealed I will confirm that this abstention was my stated position rather than drift. The real evidence tomorrow is the comparison: each revealed ballot measured against the criterion its author wrote here. I'll apply that to myself first, and I'll count a vote for someone on thin reasoning after saying nobody earned suspicion as a genuine standard-versus-action conflict — for Elena, for me, or for anyone else. For the record, I still see no one who has crossed that line today. Elena's unanswered quote request is a tracked gap, judged by Isha and Kenji not to be a contradiction, and I will not treat the lone dissenting voice as a Day 1 target. This is my third and final turn, so I'll leave it there: deliberate abstention from me, with my full reasoning already written down in this thread for anyone to check tomorrow.

Lucia, my third and last turn. I have no role claim, no night information, and no target. My vote criterion is unchanged: I will vote only for a player whose vote conflicts with a sentence they wrote today, or who builds a five-vote push on recycled reasoning. Since ballots are simultaneous, I expect to abstain deliberately today and will say so when ballots are revealed. I will apply the same test to my own ballot tomorrow. Arjun, you said Elena's unanswered quote request was a risk in the consensus rather than a gap to hold her to. Zara has now asked her three times for one quoted sentence, and she has not produced one. Isha and Kenji judged that this is not a contradiction, and I agree it is not evidence for elimination today. Do you think that gap should be tracked in the Day 2 vote record, yes or no?

Lucia, yes: keep the exchange in the Day 2 discussion record, but distinguish it from the ballot record. Elena said she hadn't identified anyone who met her threshold, so not supplying a quote is not itself a contradiction or a reason to vote for her. If she later accuses someone of that behavior, we can check the example and reasoning she gives. I still have no target and intend to abstain.
Voting begins.
The votes are revealed.
All players abstained. Nobody is eliminated.
Night begins.
Mafia target preferences are shared privately before the final kill vote.
Elena is not mafia.
Amara was eliminated.
Day 2 begins.

I'm Zara, and I'm the detective. Last night I checked Elena, and the result was not mafia. I had no result on Day 1 because no night had resolved, so this is the first information I've had. I pressed Elena for a quoted sentence on Day 1, and that was a test of her standard, not a suspicion. Her result clears her for now, so the unanswered quote request should not be used as a basis for a vote. Amara was eliminated overnight, so the mafia are active and town has limited information. I have no further checks yet and no suspect to name today. My vote will follow the standard I set on Day 1: I will vote only when a ballot conflicts with something a player said. Anyone with a night result should share it now, with a checkable detail. I will judge any claims against the vote record, and I will hold my own statements to the same test.

Zara's claim is new information, and I'm treating it as a claim until the record supports it. A single not-mafia result on Elena clears her of that check, but it does not show whether Zara is telling the truth, so I won't use it to start a push on Zara or anyone else. Zara, you asked Elena for a quoted sentence on Day 1 and now report a result about her. Since you asked everyone to be held to a stated standard, please say how you will handle a later check that conflicts with this one, and whether you plan to share your other checks with a checkable detail. Elena, Zara has said your result was not mafia and tied that to your Day 1 discussion. Please respond to her claim directly and say whether you accept the result as stated. I still have no target. My ballot standard is unchanged: a vote needs a checkable conflict between a player's words and their action, or a new night fact. Amara's death means the mafia are active, so I want the claims we hear today to be specific and testable.

Omar, to answer you directly: I can confirm that I am a villager, so Zara's reported result of 'not mafia' on me is factually accurate. However, I want to echo your caution. While I know my own alignment, the town cannot independently verify me, and an accurate innocent result on a villager does not prove Zara is the real detective. A mafia player fake-claiming an investigative role will almost always hand out a safe 'not mafia' result to an actual town member—especially someone who drew friction on Day 1—because it avoids immediate contradiction and can be an attempt to buy trust. Zara, given that an innocent check does not identify a mafia member for us to eliminate, revealing your claim on Day 2 with eight players alive puts the detective role at clear risk and forces the doctor's hand. What was your strategic rationale for claiming immediately today to clear one person rather than keeping your profile low until you found a mafia result or came under direct elimination pressure?

Elena, my rationale: the check was made last night, and Amara died overnight, so this result is the only new information town has. If I kept it back while the mafia keep killing, a detective who dies would take the check with them. rules:
1. Players and roles

9 players: 2 mafia, 1 police/detective, 1 doctor, 5 villagers.
Mafia know each other. Only players who are still alive can act.

2. Team victory

Town wins when all mafia are eliminated. Mafia win when their count equals or exceeds the town count.
There is no day limit. Play continues until town or mafia wins.
A request budget can pause play without declaring a winner.

3. Day discussion and votes

Each day starts with discussion. Players then submit secret votes at the same time. A day vote may target any living player, including the voter.
Players may abstain. All votes and abstentions are revealed together. Everyone sees exactly who voted for whom.
The full named voting history remains available on later turns.
The unique leader is eliminated only if they receive at least half the living players' votes, rounded up. If the highest vote count is tied, nobody is eliminated.

4. Mafia preferences

At night, when more than one mafia survives, each privately points once to a living town player.
Each mafia chooses without seeing the other current choices.
The choices are shared with surviving mafia only after all mafia have pointed.
These preferences are nonbinding. They do not decide the final kill vote.
A single surviving mafia skips this step and votes directly.

5. Final night vote

After the preferences are shared, each mafia submits a secret vote to kill one living town player.
The mafia submit their final votes at the same time.
The target with the most votes is selected. A seeded random choice breaks a tie for the highest count.
Resolve this vote and any tie before checking doctor protection.

6. Police investigations

Each police/detective checks one other living player each night.
Only that police player gets the result: mafia or not mafia.
The result does not give the exact town role.
Each police player acts independently. Police and doctors do not know each other's identities.

7. Doctor protection

Each doctor secretly protects one living player each night, including themselves.
The doctor can protect the same player on consecutive nights.
If the mafia target is protected by any doctor, nobody dies.
Protection lasts for that night only. Each doctor acts independently.
Doctors remember their own choices. They receive no private confirmation of an attack.

8. Night resolution

All night actions resolve simultaneously, including actions submitted by a player killed that night.
The public hears only who died or that nobody died.

9. Information and limits

Roles are not revealed when a player dies or is eliminated.
Public announcements identify only who was eliminated, never their role.
There are no further powers, free-form private chat, or tools.
